The bill would respond to a Federal Court decision and increase penalties for harming turtles and dugong.

The bill would also amend the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Act 1975 to give extra protection to dugong, marine turtles and leatherback turtles.

Environment Legislation Amendment Bill 2013 - Consideration in Detail - Keep power to make major environmental approvals with federal minister
Bills – Environment Legislation Amendment Bill 2013 – in Committee – Amendment: extend protections to all threatened species

Criticised the new Environment Minister's first legislative outing as a 'modest' piece of legislation, and condemned the government's decision to abolish the Clean Energy Finance Corporation despite its record of returning money to the budget.

Opposed the bill, citing BirdLife Australia figures that 392 kinds of fauna, including 112 bird species, are listed as threatened, warned the orange-bellied parrot population has fallen to about 45 birds, and said the bill would remove the minister's legal duty to consider conservation advice before approving mines, ports and housing developments.

Defended the bill's amendment addressing the Tarkine court case, noting the mine at the centre of the case was approved by then Labor environment minister Tony Burke anyway, and argued the change simply protects past and future ministerial decisions from being invalidated on a technical failure to record conservation advice.

Opposed the bill, accusing the government of also deferring $650 million in Murray-Darling Basin water buybacks affecting South Australia, and said ministers would no longer be required to consider environmental advice before approving mines, ports and housing developments, weakening accountability under the EPBC Act.

Supported the bill, citing Shree Minerals' iron ore mine approval being overturned by a court challenge from the Save the Tarkine coalition as evidence miners need certainty, and criticised a fresh High Court challenge to the Venture Minerals proposal timed just before Christmas.

Argued the bill is a 'stalking horse' that uses new penalties for killing turtles and dugongs to obscure removing the minister's legal duty to consider conservation advice, noting all six species of marine turtle found off Queensland are listed as threatened or endangered under the EPBC Act.

Argued the Environment Legislation Amendment Bill 2013 weakens Commonwealth environmental law by removing the ability of courts to invalidate ministerial decisions that ignore conservation advice, citing the Tarkine Forest case, but supported the bill's stronger penalties for harming turtles and dugongs and noted Labor's $7 million investment in Indigenous self-management of those species.

Opposed the Environment Legislation Amendment Bill 2013, warning it removes the requirement for ministers to consider threatened species advice like that for turtles and dugongs while simultaneously increasing penalties for illegally hunting them, and criticised the bill's retrospective effect and the delegation of environmental approval powers to state governments led by Barry O'Farrell and Campbell Newman.

Defended the Environment Legislation Amendment Bill, announcing a sunset clause protecting past ministerial decisions made up to 31 December this year from legal challenge, said the bill triples financial penalties for poaching turtles and dugongs, and rejected proposed Greens amendments as risking delay and duplication under the one-stop-shop approvals process.

The speaker presented the Environment Legislation Amendment Bill 2013 to provide legal certainty for past conservation decisions under the EPBC Act and triple criminal and civil penalties for poaching and illegal trade of turtles and dugong. The Infrastructure Australia Amendment Bill 2013 was introduced to restructure the agency as an independent authority, conduct five-yearly audits, develop a 15-year infrastructure plan, and review all Commonwealth-funded projects over $100 million. The Migration Amendment (Regaining Control Over Australia’s Protection Obligations) Bill 2013 removes the complementary protection criterion from the Migration Act, reverting to an administrative process for assessing non-refoulement obligations under the CAT and ICCPR, while maintaining those obligations.

Introduced amendments tripling penalties for killing, injuring or trading turtles and dugongs in Commonwealth marine areas and the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park, and announced a $5.3 million protection plan including $2 million for an Australian Crime Commission illegal fishing investigation and $2 million for Indigenous ranger programs.
